title: Stride: Scale-Aware Multi-Agent Evolutionary Refinement for Infographic Generation

paper.title: Stride: Scale-Aware Multi-Agent Evolutionary Refinement for Infographic Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Infographic generation challenges text-to-image models because a single image must satisfy numerous visual, textual, and semantic constraints. Iterative agentic refinement with a multimodal verifier is a natural remedy, but existing methods face a scale mismatch: local edits cannot correct global composition errors, while full regeneration may destroy already-correct regions. We introduce Stride , a constraint-grounded multi-agent framework that treats refinement over any frozen generator as a history-aware evolution strategy. Stride separates constraint evaluation—whether each requirement is satisfied—from visual grounding—where and how it is violated. It then routes global revisions to a composer subagent and local corrections to a retoucher subagent. Each subagent conducts internal planning and generates multiple candidates, while Stride accepts a candidate only when it improves the verifier score, reducing regression across iterations.
Because stochastic generators and imperfect verifiers make any single step unreliable, it is this combination of scale-aware routing, per-step redundancy, and monotonic acceptance that yields stable improvement across iterations.
With fully open-weight generator–verifier systems, Stride outperforms proprietary systems including Nano-Banana-2.0 and Seedream-5.0-Pro on BizGenEval, matches GPT-Image-2.0 and surpasses Seedream-5.0-Pro on IGenBench, and achieves a new state-of-the-art score on WISE, while substantially outperforming existing agentic methods across all evaluated benchmarks 1 1 1 Code is available at https://github.com/SJTUSAI/Stride . .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) generation has made remarkable progress in producing visually compelling images, but generating reliable, information-rich visual content remains challenging ( Li et al., 2026a ; Tang et al., 2026 ) . Infographics are a representative example ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , where text, numerical facts, charts, and spatial layout must work together to convey information correctly. A single incorrect value, malformed label, or inconsistent visual relationship can compromise the reliability of the entire infographic ( Li et al., 2026b ; Zhu et al., 2026a ) . However, existing generation paradigms primarily optimize image synthesis without explicitly verifying whether generated content satisfies its underlying constraints. Recent models have made significant progress in infographic generation. Closed-source systems such as Nano-Banana 2.0 ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) and GPT-Image 2.0 ( OpenAI, 2026b ) exhibit strong visual generation capabilities, while open-source models such as ERNIE-Image ( Liu et al., 2026 ) and Infographic-V2 ( Diao et al., 2026 ) make infographic generation increasingly accessible and specialized. Beyond direct generation, recent agent-based approaches, including PaperBanana ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) , AutoFigure ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) , and PromptEnhancer ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , employ planning, feedback, and iterative refinement to further enhance generation quality. Nevertheless, existing approaches remain largely focused on visual plausibility and overall quality, with limited ability to explicitly verify fine-grained information constraints, localize their violations, and perform targeted correction. Distilling these limitations, we identify three key challenges in current agentic generation and refinement methods: • Insufficiently Grounded Feedback. Holistic scores and coarse critiques provide limited guidance for targeted correction. Constraint-level judgments alone may still leave the location and nature of a failure unclear. • Mismatch between Error and Edit Scales. Infographic errors range from global composition failures to localized text defects. A single revision mechanism cannot address both effectively: local edits have limited structural reach, while full-image regeneration can disrupt correct content when only a small correction is needed. • Unreliable Progress across Iterations. A revision may fix one requirement while violating another, and stochastic generation makes individual proposals unreliable. To address these challenges, we introduce Stride , a training-free multi-agent framework for scale-aware evolutionary refinement over frozen text-to-image generators. Stride separates rubric-based verification from visual grounding, combining constraint-level judgments with spatial evidence to guide targeted correction. A trajectory-aware lead editor uses this feedback and prior attempts to route revisions to a composer for global regeneration or a retoucher for localized text and formula correction. Each selected sub-agent proposes multiple candidates, and a ( 1 + λ ) (1+\lambda) -evolution strategy retains the current champion unless a candidate improves its verifier score, allowing exploration while limiting regression. Stride outperforms Nano-Banana-2.0 and Seedream-5.0-Pro on BizGenEval, matches GPT-Image-2.0 and surpasses Seedream-5.0-Pro on IGenBench, and achieves a new state-of-the-art score on WISE, while substantially outperforming existing agentic methods across all evaluated benchmarks. Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce Stride , a training-free framework that formulates infographic generation as scale-aware evolutionary refinement over frozen generators, adapting the scope of correction to the errors in the current image. • We develop a refinement loop that separates rubric verification from spatial grounding, uses refinement history to guide global or local corrections, and combines multiple proposals with verifier-guided champion retention to reduce regression. • Experiments show that Stride outperforms contemporary agentic methods and selected proprietary systems, while demonstrating strong scalability across different generators and benchmarks. Extensive experiments characterize the contributions of grounding, execution routes, and champion evolution.

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Infographic Generation. Early text-to-image methods ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Diao et al., 2026 ) progressively improved the rendering of accurate and legible text, and later systems ( Gao et al., 2025 ; OpenAI, 2026b ) extended this to multi-layer posters and commercial visuals. ChartGalaxy ( Li et al., 2026b ) and InfoChartQA ( Xie et al., 2026 ) study chart understanding and chart-related visual reasoning, while BizGenEval ( Li et al., 2026a ) and IGenBench ( Tang et al., 2026 ) evaluate whether generated visuals satisfy infographic-specified requirements. Proprietary models ( Google DeepMind, 2025c ; Google DeepMind, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2025 ; OpenAI, 2026b ) have shown strong performance, but they still struggle to simultaneously satisfy a large number of discrete requirements and factual constraints in infographic generation. Open-weight models ( Diao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Tang et al., 2026 ) fall further behind when faced with the dense constraints imposed by infographic requirements. Stride addresses this challenge through iterative dual-route evaluation and scale-aware refinement, enabling open-weight generators to match or even surpass proprietary models on this sophisticated task. Figure 1: Overview of Stride . From K K initial samples, Stride selects a champion and refines it for t t rounds. Each round performs evolutionary refinement and agent state update through dual-route evaluation: the verifier scores candidate images against the rubrics, while the perceptor provides visual grounding of the observed failures. The lead editor then analyzes the agent state and refinement trajectory to route the champion to either the composer for global redraw or the retoucher for local editing. The generated candidates are then re-evaluated, and the champion is updated only when a candidate improves the verifier score. Repeating this process yields the final champion. Agentic Augmentation. Agentic methods ( Wang et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) enhance prompts by retrieving implicit details or reference images to condition generation, but their one-shot rewriting paradigm provides limited constraint enforcement and may overwrite content that is already correct. Methods such as Ag3 ( Hahn et al., 2024 ) and AutoFigure ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) use editable graphs or SVGs to specify image layouts and conduct fixed-round layout-guided refinement. However, their reliance on proprietary models obscures whether gains come from the agentic framework or the base models, which also limits compatibility with most open-weight text-to-image generators. ReflectionFlow ( Zhuo et al., 2025 ) , T2I-Copilot ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and PaperBanana ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) use verifier feedback to assess and refine generated outputs, but the absence of explicit rubric grounding makes failures under-specified, and their reliance on prompt revision or full-image regeneration can disrupt already correct regions and limit reliable improvement. Guided by dual-route evaluated failed rubrics and an evolution strategy, Stride adaptively combines global regeneration with local editing to target specific errors, addressing the above limitations while ensuring stable improvement.

sections.heading: 3.1 Overview
sections.text: As shown in Figure 1 , Stride is a training-free multi-agent framework designed to iteratively refine images produced by any black-box text-to-image generator G ⁡ ( P , z ) G(P,z) , where P P is a prompt query and z z a noise sample. We observe that generation failures often arise in two opposite regimes: global/compositional errors that local editing cannot repair, and localized residual errors that full re-generation would only perturb. Stride therefore operates over a scale-aware execution space with two complementary sub-agents – a composer that globally resamples the frozen generator and a retoucher that locally edits the current champion. The per-round choice between them is made by a central lead editor , which selects and guides the sub-agent based on the current agent state and the observations from a dual-route evaluation module. The core components of Stride are: (1) Dual-Route Evaluation. Stride uses internal evaluations to drive iterative image refinement. Notably, it decouples evaluation into two complementary MLLM-based modules with distinct roles. The verifier performs closed-form judgment, scoring fine-grained semantic compliance against a rubric set. The perceptor performs open-form grounding, extracting region-level structured descriptions (object locations, rendered text, attribute–region bindings, etc.) that help localize where a failed rubric is violated. Separating judgment from grounding lets each module specialize, and supplies the editor with the spatial evidence a pass/fail score alone cannot provide. (2) Trajectory-Aware Lead Editor . As the central controller, the lead editor maintains a running state of candidate history, prior discriminator observations and failure mode, and the detailed editing history. Rather than simple prompt rewriting, it performs reflective trajectory analysis, makes a decision on which actor (composer or retoucher) to invoke, and then formulates prompt updates for the selected actor that target to address previous failures. (3) Scale-Aware Execution Sub-Agent Space . To prevent generative drift during iterative image generation, Stride operates over a dual-branch action space defined by two sub-agents. The composer explores the global generative manifold by rewriting the prompt and then resampling the image generator G G , while the retoucher identifies localized editing needs and invokes specialized computer-vision tools, guarded by the perceptor’s spatial grounding. The output of each editing action is then admitted or rejected under an evolution strategy. The current champion enters a new round of image refinement, until the iteration budget is exhausted.

sections.heading: 3.3 Dual-Route Evaluation

This module decouples image quality assessment into semantic rubric verification and structured perceptual evidence extraction. Rubric-Based Verifier. Visual Grounding via the Perceptor. While the verifier issues rubric-level pass/fail judgments, the perceptor grounds those judgments spatially: it localizes objects, reads rendered text, and reports region-level attributes (Appendix J.2 ). This grounding resolves where and how a constraint fails, which the retoucher needs to target its local edits. The perceptor is applied to every round candidate alongside the verifier, but champion selection is driven by the verifier score S S alone. After each round, only the grounding of the admitted champion is written into the state as E t = E ⁡ ( I t ) E_{t}=E(I_{t}) . It’s also worth noting that we tested using specialized detection/OCR tools as perceptor and they underperformed a strong MLLM model like Kimi-K3 (Appendix F.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.4 Trajectory-Aware Lead Editor
sections.text: A single editing mechanism is often insufficient for iterative image refinement. When the current image contains global semantic or compositional failures, local editing is too weak to recover the missing structure. Conversely, when only a small subset of attributes remains incorrect, full-image regeneration introduces unnecessary drift. To balance these two regimes, Stride operates over a scale-aware action space with two complementary operators: global redraw, executed by the composer, and local refinement, executed by the retoucher. The lead editor serves as the central controller of Stride . At round t t , it reads the current agent state S t = ( I t , V t , E t , H t ) S_{t}=\bigl(I_{t},\ V_{t},\ E_{t},\ H_{t}\bigr) and performs reflective trajectory analysis. It then determines which editing sub-agent to invoke next and what editing guidance G t G_{t} to pass to it (Appendix J.3 ). The lead editor invokes the composer for global failure modes, including missing objects, incorrect layouts, and compositional errors that jointly violate multiple constraints. It invokes the retoucher when the residual errors are localized and spatially addressable, such as text-rendering errors, minor attribute mismatches, or confined visual defects.

It first queries the perceptor for region-level groundings B ⁡ ( I t ) B(I_{t}) : indexed OCR text blocks that localize content, each paired with the checklist questions it fails. Each surviving branch is realized by the SVG toolbox, which implements RenderEdit \mathrm{RenderEdit} locally: it masks the selected box with the sampled background color, renders the correction as a transparent PNG, and recovers the original typographic attributes so that the edit aligns seamlessly while the surrounding layout stays fixed. sections.heading: 4.1 Benchmarks and Setup
sections.text: Benchmarks. To fairly compare Stride with contemporary proprietary and open-source T2I models as well as agentic generation methods, we evaluate its infographic generation and refinement capability on two large-scale public benchmarks: (1) BizGenEval ( Li et al., 2026a ) , (2) IGenBench ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . To evaluate the scalability of Stride , we further conduct general-purpose, non-infographic-specific experiments on the (3) WISE ( Niu et al., 2025 ) dataset. Setup. Stride uses Kimi-K3 ( Kimi et al., 2026a ) as the lead editor, perceptor, composer, and retoucher, with open-weight text-to-image generators including ERNIE-Image ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , Infographic-V2 ( Diao et al., 2026 ) , and Qwen-Image-2512 ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . The verifier is the open-weight Qwen3.5-397B-A17B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) model. The agent runs for at most t = 3 t=3 iterations under a ( 1 + λ ) (1+\lambda) -evolution strategy with λ = 4 \lambda=4 ; the initial champion I 0 I_{0} is selected from the best-of- K = 6 K=6 samples at t = 0 t=0 . The composer samples M = 4 M=4 candidates from the frozen generator, and the retoucher launches N = 4 N=4 parallel local editing branches. We set the internal confidence thresholds to τ c ∗ = 0.7 \tau_{c}^{*}=0.7 for the composer and τ r ∗ = 0.8 \tau_{r}^{*}=0.8 for the retoucher. Final benchmark evaluation uses the corresponding official evaluator for each benchmark (Appendix B ).

Detailed results are provided in Appendix D.2 . Candidate Exploration. Increasing the candidate pool from Best-of-1 to Best-of-6 (Table 3 (1)-(2)) raises the BizGenEval average from 28.0 to 34.7, but the result remains far below the full system’s score of 51.1. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented Stride , a training-free multi-agent framework that formulates infographic generation as scale-aware evolutionary refinement over frozen text-to-image generators. Stride separates rubric-based verification from spatial grounding, routes failures to either global composition or local retouching according to their scale, and admits only candidates that improve verifier-scored constraint satisfaction under an evolution strategy. Across BizGenEval, IGenBench and WISE, Stride consistently improves open-weight generators, outperforms prior agentic enhancement methods, and matches or surpasses proprietary systems. We hope this work inspires future advancements in agentic infographic generation and refinement.

sections.heading: Appendix B Benchmark Details
sections.text: Table 6: Quantitative overview of the public benchmarks used in our evaluation. Final reporting follows each benchmark’s official evaluator and metrics. Benchmark Scale Coverage Final eval. units Metrics BizGenEval 400 prompts 5 domains × \times 4 capabilities = 20 tasks 8,000 checklist judgments Score, Accuracy IGenBench 600 cases 30 infographic types in 6 categories 5,259 QA judgments Q-ACC, I-ACC WISE 1,000 prompts 3 domains, 25 subdomains, 6 report categories 3,000 dimension scores WiScore We evaluate Stride on three large-scale public benchmarks that provide complementary tests of infographic and structured visual generation. BizGenEval focuses on commercial visual documents with dense text, layout, attribute, and knowledge constraints. IGenBench targets text-to-infographic reliability, especially faithful data encoding and end-to-end constraint satisfaction. WISE evaluates knowledge-grounded generation from indirect semantic cues. Table 6 summarizes the scale, coverage, and evaluation protocol of each benchmark. BizGenEval. BizGenEval ( Li et al., 2026a ) crosses five professional content domains (slides, charts, webpages, posters, and scientific figures) with four capability dimensions of text rendering, layout control, attribute binding, and knowledge-based reasoning. The prompt set contains 300 content-based prompts derived from real-world commercial visual materials and 100 knowledge-based prompts covering physics, chemistry, mathematics, history, and arts. Each prompt is paired with 20 task-specific verification questions, and final scores are computed from MLLM checklist judgments on easy and hard tracks. BizGenEval uses Gemini-3-Flash-Preview ( Google DeepMind, 2025b ) as its official evaluator. BizGenEval’s official code reports two closely related checklist-based metrics. Let q q denote the number of questions in a track and let Q err Q_{\mathrm{err}} be the number of incorrectly answered questions. The (1) checklist accuracy is Accuracy = q − Q err q . \mathrm{Accuracy}=\frac{q-Q_{\mathrm{err}}}{q}. Following the leaderboard protocol, BizGenEval-related results report the official error score, unless otherwise stated. IGenBench. IGenBench ( Tang et al., 2026 ) contains 600 curated test cases spanning 30 infographic types, its evaluation decomposes each infographic specification into atomic yes/no verification questions. These questions cover 10 types of infographic elements (Title & Subtitle, Chart/Diagram Type, Decorative/Non-data Elements, Annotations & Callouts, Axes & Scales, Legend & Category Mapping, Data Marks, Data Completeness, Data Ordering, and Data Encoding). IGenBench uses Gemini-2.5-Pro ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) as its official evaluator, reporting both Q-ACC, which measures individual constraint satisfaction, and I-ACC, which requires all questions for an infographic to be answered correctly. The official released dataset contains 5,259 atomic yes/no verification questions, including 3,730 prompt-derived questions and 1,529 expert-informed seed questions. WISE. WISE ( Niu et al., 2025 ) evaluates world-knowledge-informed image generation. Unlike benchmarks that use direct prompts, WISE avoids naming the target entity explicitly and instead describes it through clues, relations, or conditions. WISE contains 1,000 prompts across 25 subdomains in three major areas, including 400 cultural prompts, 300 spatio-temporal prompts, and 300 natural-science prompts, while the latter two are further divided into time, space, biology, physics, and chemistry categories. WISE uses WiScore as its metric and uses GPT-4o-2024-05-13 ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) as its official evaluator. WiScore combines consistency, realism, and aesthetic quality, with default weights of 0.7, 0.2, and 0.1, respectively, and normalizes the weighted score to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] .

A line of retrieval-augmented planning methods, exemplified by PromptEnhancer ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , Mind-Brush ( He et al., 2026 ) , Gen-Searcher ( Feng et al., 2026 ) , and GenEvolve ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , augments text-to-image generation by searching for implicit prompt content or retrieving reference images to condition the generator. These methods subsequently reorganize the prompt through a planning stage, yielding an enhanced prompt intended to improve generation quality. Nevertheless, these approaches are fundamentally limited to one-shot prompt rewriting. As a result, they not only fall short of enforcing the desired constraints, but can also compromise previously verified correct content. (2) Layout-Augmented Planning Methods. Methods such as Ag3 ( Hahn et al., 2024 ) and AutoFigure ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) augment generation with explicit layout planning, typically via editable graphs or SVGs, followed by fixed-round layout-guided refinement. However, their reliance on closed-source frontier models throughout generation and optimization obscures whether the gains stem from the agentic design or from the underlying models. Their extra layout-control components also limit compatibility with most open-source text-to-image generators. (3) Analysis-Evaluation Methods. Methods represented by ReflectionFlow ( Zhuo et al., 2025 ) , T2I-Copilot ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and PaperBanana ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) refine generated images under the guidance of a verifier that evaluates the current output. Yet the verifier feedback is typically not rubric-grounded, making it difficult to translate detected failures into precise and actionable corrections. In addition, their execution space is narrow, usually restricted to prompt revision or full regeneration. As a result, full-image regeneration can introduce regressions by altering already verified correct regions, leaving limited room for reliable improvement. These existing systems improve over single-pass generation in many settings, but dense infographic generation requires additional mechanisms. In particular, a refinement loop must identify which rubrics failed, decide whether the failure should be addressed by global regeneration or localized editing, and prevent later revisions from degrading constraints that were already satisfied. Stride addresses these limitations and demonstrates clear advantages. We compare these agentic methods in Table 7 . For each representative method, we record whether it uses web search, rubric feedback as refinement state, global redrawing, local editing, iterative refinement, and champion admission, and we report the access profile of the agent backbone, base generator, and verifier. For Stride , all components are open-weight, reducing attribution ambiguity and making the reported gains reflect the framework rather than proprietary model strength. The failed rubrics returned by dual-route evaluation guide retrieval, planning, and editing, allowing each refinement step to address the concrete errors present in the current image. During iterations, Stride operates in a scale-aware execution space, adaptively combining global regeneration with local editing so that the two serve complementary roles rather than conflicting alternatives. Finally, a ( 1 + λ ) (1+\lambda) -evolution strategy accepts a proposal only when it strictly improves the current champion, ensuring monotonic and non-regressive refinement across rounds. sections.heading: D.1 Extended Main Results
sections.text: Table 8 extends the BizGenEval results by reporting both hard and easy scores for each visual domain, capability, and their average. This provides a more comprehensive view of Stride ’s performance: the hard track reflects performance on more demanding requirements, while the easy track complements it by showing how well each method handles less challenging cases. On the hard track, Stride consistently improves its base generator across all reported domains and capabilities. With ERNIE-Image, Stride raises the average score from 28.0 to 51.1, a gain of 23.1 points. With Infographic-V2, it raises the score from 41.1 to 69.5, a gain of 28.4 points. The improvements also extend to the easy track, where the corresponding averages increase from 55.2 to 73.7 (+18.5) and from 63.7 to 84.2 (+20.5), respectively. For example, with Infographic-V2, the hard scores for layout, attribute, text, and knowledge improve by 20.4, 23.2, 16.2, and 54.0 points, respectively. These results show that the gains are not confined to visual presentation, but also include capabilities related to satisfying specified attributes, rendering text, and incorporating relevant knowledge. Stride also substantially outperforms the listed prior agentic frameworks when paired with the same base generator. On the hard track, its average exceeds the strongest corresponding baseline by 23.4 points with ERNIE-Image (51.1 vs. 27.7) and by 26.3 points with Infographic-V2 (69.5 vs. 43.2). The advantage is also present on the easy track, with gains of 15.1 points (73.7 vs. 58.6) and 13.7 points (84.2 vs. 70.5), respectively. Thus, the improvements are not limited to a single difficulty track or a single base generator. Finally, Stride (Infographic-V2) surpasses several proprietary models on the hard average, including Seedream-5.0 (48.8), Seedream-5.0-Pro (65.7), and Nano-Banana-2.0 (68.5), with a score of 69.5. It also exceeds these models on the easy average where applicable: its score of 84.2 is higher than Seedream-5.0 (79.2) and Seedream-5.0-Pro (82.8), though lower than Nano-Banana-2.0 (92.5). These comparisons indicate that an open-weight generator combined with Stride can outperform a number of proprietary systems, particularly on the more demanding hard track. Scale-Aware Sub-Agent Preferences. Table 10 further breaks down the lead editor’s preferences for the composer and retoucher by generator, dimension, and iteration. The preferences vary substantially across dimensions, rather than consistently favoring a single sub-agent. For both generators, the composer is strongly preferred for layout (93.7% overall for ERNIE-Image and 94.6% for Infographic-V2) and is also preferred for attribute and knowledge. In contrast, the retoucher is preferred for text, accounting for 84.1% of the decisions with ERNIE-Image and 81.9% with Infographic-V2. This pattern is consistent with the different strengths of the two routes: broader composition changes are more often selected for layout-level issues, while localized editing is more often selected for text-related corrections. The preference distributions also vary across iterations and generators. For ERNIE-Image, the overall composer preference remains relatively stable across the three rounds (58.9%, 58.7%, and 57.6%), while for Infographic-V2 it rises from 63.6% in the first round to 72.4% in the third. The dimension-level trends are not uniform: for example, the retoucher remains the majority choice for text in every round for both generators, whereas the composer remains strongly preferred for layout. These differences indicate that the lead editor’s routing behavior depends on the generator, the error dimension, and the refinement round, rather than following a fixed composer-only or retoucher-only policy. Together with the improved results of the combined system, these preference patterns provide evidence for the scale-aware operation of Stride .

sections.heading: F.2 Choice of Perceptor
sections.text: The perceptor is an important but replaceable component in Stride . Its role is not to decide whether a candidate should be admitted, as champion selection is still governed by the rubric-based verifier score. Instead, the perceptor provides open-form visual grounding for the lead editor and the retoucher, including visible text blocks, their bounding boxes, and whether the rendered text appears corrupted. This distinction matters because the retoucher can only repair a failure that has been localized. The choice of perception backbone therefore bounds the practical effectiveness of local editing, but it is not a fixed assumption of the framework. Protocol. We select the default perceptor backbone through a small, stratified agreement study and practical closed-loop verification. The study uses 20 generated infographics sampled across the five BizGenEval domains and two base generators, ERNIE-Image and Infographic-V2. Each candidate perceptor backend is asked to return visible text blocks and normalized bounding boxes. Since generated images do not come with ground-truth text-box annotations, we use Gemini-3-Flash-Preview as a proxy reference after sanity-checking its localization behavior against a dedicated PP-OCRv5 server ( Cui et al., 2026 ) . PP-OCRv5 server is therefore included in the table as a cross-check/reference OCR baseline, rather than as the perception backbone selected for Stride . Table 16 shows that no single backend dominates every criterion. PP-OCRv5 has the strongest box coverage and the smallest anchor offsets, which confirms that the cross-check OCR baseline is a strong text localizer. However, its transcription agreement is substantially weaker than the strongest MLLM backends: its exact-match rate is 0.590, compared with 0.721 for Kimi-K3 ( Kimi et al., 2026a ) and 0.751 for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) . Qwen3.5-397B-A17B achieves the best matched-text similarity, but its recall and precision are much lower and its P90 anchor offset is nearly three times that of Kimi-K3, indicating a heavier tail of localization failures. Kimi-K3 provides the most balanced open-weight tradeoff: its A-F1 is close to the OCR cross-check baseline PP-OCRv5, its mean IoU is comparable, and its transcription agreement is much higher than the conventional OCR baseline, including PP-OCRv5 and LocateAnything ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Why OCR Alone is Insufficient. The perceptor in Stride is not a generic OCR module. It must supply spatial evidence that is useful for deciding whether a failed rubric can be repaired locally. Conventional OCR and detection models ( Zhou, 2024 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) are optimized to find text-like regions and transcribe them, but generated infographics often contain pseudo-text artifacts: glyphs that look like text locally but are misspelled, structurally broken, or semantically nonsensical in context. In such cases, as shown in Figure 4 , a pure OCR system (like PP-OCRv5 in Figure 4 (d) or LocateAnything in Figure 4 (h)) can return precise boxes around corrupted glyphs and treat them as normal readable text. These false-positive text blocks are harmful for the retoucher, because they create repair targets that appear well localized while failing to represent reliable semantic evidence. An MLLM perceptor is better aligned with this use case because it jointly considers the box, the transcription, and the surrounding linguistic and visual context, including whether the text should be marked as garbled. Backbone Choice. We choose Kimi-K3 as the default perceptor for reasons beyond single-call localization agreement. First, it offers the best overall balance between localization coverage and text understanding among the open-weight candidates in Table 16 . Second, the rubric-based verifier in our default stack uses a Qwen-series model. Reusing the same model family for perception would increase the risk of correlated errors between the grounding signal and the verification signal, weakening the benefit of the dual-route design. Third, Stride does not rely on a single perception sample. Each refinement round aggregates 4 to 10 OCR/perception samples, and rollback triggers resampling in later rounds. This repeated-sampling design directly mitigates the long-tail localization failures observed in single-call diagnostics.

sections.text: Evolution Strategy Experiment Setup. Table 17 compares alternative champion-evolution strategies on BizGenEval. We use the Hard track as the primary evaluation protocol and report Easy-track scores for reference. The comparison separates two decisions in champion evolution. First, the pick decision selects the best candidate within the current new champion candidate set. Second, the admission decision determines whether the picked candidate should replace the incumbent champion. In the default ( 1 + 4 ) (1+4) -evolution strategy, both decisions are made by the Qwen3.5-397B-A17B verifier. The oracle-admission variant keeps Qwen3.5-397B-A17B for within-round candidate selection but uses the Gemini-3-Flash-Preview evaluator for admission. The full-oracle variant uses Gemini-3-Flash-Preview for both candidate selection and admission. Champion Candidates. Among the non-oracle variants, our default ( 1 + 4 ) (1+4) -evolution strategy achieves the highest average hard score, reaching 51.1. Increasing the candidate count improves both forced-replacement and evolution strategies: the forced-replacement score increases from 39.4 for ( 1 , 1 ) (1,1) to 45.4 for ( 1 , 4 ) (1,4) , while the evolution strategy score increases from 45.6 for ( 1 + 1 ) (1+1) to 51.1 for ( 1 + 4 ) (1+4) . Thus, generating multiple proposals provides a substantial search benefit under both admission rules. Incumbent Retention. Incumbent retention provides an additional and independent benefit. With one candidate, the evolution strategy improves the hard average from 39.4 for forced replacement ( 1 , 1 ) (1,1) to 45.6 for ( 1 + 1 ) (1+1) , a gain of 6.2 points. With four candidates, the corresponding improvement is 5.7 points, from 45.4 for forced replacement ( 1 , 4 ) (1,4) to 51.1 for ( 1 + 4 ) (1+4) . Therefore, the performance of the proposed strategy is not explained by increased candidate sampling alone: it also depends on rejecting non-improving updates and preserving a strong incumbent. Selection Methods. Random selection reaches an average hard score of 40.4, which is substantially below the proposed ( 1 + 4 ) (1+4) strategy. It slightly outperforms forced replacement ( 1 , 1 ) (1,1) , which reaches 39.4, indicating that random replacement can occasionally benefit from stochastic diversity. However, it remains well below the strategies that combine multiple proposals with score-guided selection and incumbent retention. This result suggests that repeated stochastic modification alone is insufficient for reliable refinement. Oracle Experiments in Evolution Strategy. We also conducted oracle evaluations in our evolution-strategy comparison. In Table 17 , replacing only the Qwen-based admission decision with the Gemini-based benchmark evaluator increases the Hard average from 51.1 to 56.9, a gain of 5.8 points, while the corresponding Easy score increases from 73.7 to 74.7. Because within-round candidate selection remains Qwen-based in this setting, this improvement isolates the effect of the admission decision. The result indicates that the default verifier sometimes accepts inferior updates or rejects beneficial ones, with the largest Hard-score gains appearing in Knowledge (+7.6), Attribute (+6.0), and Text (+5.8). The full-oracle variant, which uses Gemini for both within-round candidate selection and admission, further increases the Hard average to 64.4. This is 7.5 points above oracle admission and 13.3 points above the default ( 1 + 4 ) (1+4) strategy. Since admission is already controlled by Gemini in both oracle variants, the additional gap isolates errors in Qwen’s within-round candidate ranking. The largest additional gain is observed for Knowledge, which improves from 41.6 under oracle admission to 54.8 under the full oracle. These results show that both candidate ranking and incumbent admission contribute to the remaining performance gap. Overall, the comparison supports the ( 1 + λ ) (1+\lambda) -evolution strategy as a central component of Stride . Multiple candidates improve the search space explored in each refinement round, while incumbent retention prevents the system from replacing a strong champion with a lower-quality proposal. The oracle results further show that the effectiveness of this mechanism is bounded by the quality of the verifier used for candidate ranking and admission.

sections.text: Figures 5 and 6 present additional qualitative results on infographic generation. Across the shown examples, Stride produces more complete and coherent infographics than existing agentic methods, with better preservation of the requested layout, attributes, text, and semantic content. In contrast, the compared methods more frequently exhibit missing or distorted text, incorrect element arrangements, and unresolved prompt constraints. These examples further illustrate the benefit of Stride ’s rubric-guided diagnosis, scale-aware execution, and iterative champion refinement. The consistent improvements across these examples suggest that Stride ’s refinement mechanism is not tied to a particular visual domain and can generalize to tasks with prompt-derived requirements. sections.heading: Appendix I Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: Stride has two limitations that suggest directions for future work. First, although the open-weight configuration achieves competitive results, refinement remains dependent on the reliability of rubric verification and spatial grounding. Monotonic admission applies to the internal verifier score and does not guarantee improvement under independent evaluation. Our diagnostic experiments indicate room for improvement in these components, which the modular framework can readily accommodate. Better-calibrated verification and more precise grounding could further strengthen candidate selection and targeted correction. Second, the current retoucher focuses on text and formula replacement within localized regions, enabling targeted corrections while preserving the surrounding content. Changes to chart geometry or spatial relationships currently rely on the composer’s global regeneration. Extending local refinement to structured visual elements would allow a broader range of errors to be corrected without redrawing the entire image. A promising direction is to jointly edit labels and their associated visual marks, further extending the benefits of scale-aware refinement.

Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Email: angelayang@sjtu.edu.cn Abstract Infographic generation challenges text-to-image models because a single image must satisfy numerous visual, textual, and semantic constraints. Iterative agentic refinement with a multimodal verifier is a natural remedy, but existing methods face a scale mismatch: local edits cannot correct global composition errors, while full regeneration may destroy already-correct regions. We introduce Stride , a constraint-grounded multi-agent framework that treats refinement over any frozen generator as a history-aware evolution strategy. Stride separates constraint evaluation—whether each requirement is satisfied—from visual grounding—where and how it is violated. It then routes global revisions to a composer subagent and local corrections to a retoucher subagent. Each subagent conducts internal planning and generates multiple candidates, while Stride accepts a candidate only when it improves the verifier score, reducing regression across iterations. Because stochastic generators and imperfect verifiers make any single step unreliable, it is this combination of scale-aware routing, per-step redundancy, and monotonic acceptance that yields stable improvement across iterations. With fully open-weight generator–verifier systems, Stride outperforms proprietary systems including Nano-Banana-2.0 and Seedream-5.0-Pro on BizGenEval, matches GPT-Image-2.0 and surpasses Seedream-5.0-Pro on IGenBench, and achieves a new state-of-the-art score on WISE, while substantially outperforming existing agentic methods across all evaluated benchmarks 1 1 1 Code is available at https://github.com/SJTUSAI/Stride . . 1 Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) generation has made remarkable progress in producing visually compelling images, but generating reliable, information-rich visual content remains challenging ( Li et al., 2026a ; Tang et al., 2026 ) . Infographics are a representative example ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , where text, numerical facts, charts, and spatial layout must work together to convey information correctly. A single incorrect value, malformed label, or inconsistent visual relationship can compromise the reliability of the entire infographic ( Li et al., 2026b ; Zhu et al., 2026a ) . However, existing generation paradigms primarily optimize image synthesis without explicitly verifying whether generated content satisfies its underlying constraints. Recent models have made significant progress in infographic generation. Closed-source systems such as Nano-Banana 2.0 ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) and GPT-Image 2.0 ( OpenAI, 2026b ) exhibit strong visual generation capabilities, while open-source models such as ERNIE-Image ( Liu et al., 2026 ) and Infographic-V2 ( Diao et al., 2026 ) make infographic generation increasingly accessible and specialized. Beyond direct generation, recent agent-based approaches, including PaperBanana ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) , AutoFigure ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) , and PromptEnhancer ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , employ planning, feedback, and iterative refinement to further enhance generation quality. Nevertheless, existing approaches remain largely focused on visual plausibility and overall quality, with limited ability to explicitly verify fine-grained information constraints, localize their violations, and perform targeted correction. Distilling these limitations, we identify three key challenges in current agentic generation and refinement methods: • Insufficiently Grounded Feedback. Holistic scores and coarse critiques provide limited guidance for targeted correction. Constraint-level judgments alone may still leave the location and nature of a failure unclear. • Mismatch between Error and Edit Scales. Infographic errors range from global composition failures to localized text defects. A single revision mechanism cannot address both effectively: local edits have limited structural reach, while full-image regeneration can disrupt correct content when only a small correction is needed. • Unreliable Progress across Iterations. A revision may fix one requirement while violating another, and stochastic generation makes individual proposals unreliable. To address these challenges, we introduce Stride , a training-free multi-agent framework for scale-aware evolutionary refinement over frozen text-to-image generators. Stride separates rubric-based verification from visual grounding, combining constraint-level judgments with spatial evidence to guide targeted correction. A trajectory-aware lead editor uses this feedback and prior attempts to route revisions to a composer for global regeneration or a retoucher for localized text and formula correction. Each selected sub-agent proposes multiple candidates, and a ( 1 + λ ) (1+\lambda) -evolution strategy retains the current champion unless a candidate improves its verifier score, allowing exploration while limiting regression. Stride outperforms Nano-Banana-2.0 and Seedream-5.0-Pro on BizGenEval, matches GPT-Image-2.0 and surpasses Seedream-5.0-Pro on IGenBench, and achieves a new state-of-the-art score on WISE, while substantially outperforming existing agentic methods across all evaluated benchmarks. Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce Stride , a training-free framework that formulates infographic generation as scale-aware evolutionary refinement over frozen generators, adapting the scope of correction to the errors in the current image. • We develop a refinement loop that separates rubric verification from spatial grounding, uses refinement history to guide global or local corrections, and combines multiple proposals with verifier-guided champion retention to reduce regression. • Experiments show that Stride outperforms contemporary agentic methods and selected proprietary systems, while demonstrating strong scalability across different generators and benchmarks. Extensive experiments characterize the contributions of grounding, execution routes, and champion evolution. 2 Related Works Infographic Generation. Early text-to-image methods ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Diao et al., 2026 ) progressively improved the rendering of accurate and legible text, and later systems ( Gao et al., 2025 ; OpenAI, 2026b ) extended this to multi-layer posters and commercial visuals. ChartGalaxy ( Li et al., 2026b ) and InfoChartQA ( Xie et al., 2026 ) study chart understanding and chart-related visual reasoning, while BizGenEval ( Li et al., 2026a ) and IGenBench ( Tang et al., 2026 ) evaluate whether generated visuals satisfy infographic-specified requirements. Proprietary models ( Google DeepMind, 2025c ; Google DeepMind, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2025 ; OpenAI, 2026b ) have shown strong performance, but they still struggle to simultaneously satisfy a large number of discrete requirements and factual constraints in infographic generation. Open-weight models ( Diao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Tang et al., 2026 ) fall further behind when faced with the dense constraints imposed by infographic requirements. Stride addresses this challenge through iterative dual-route evaluation and scale-aware refinement, enabling open-weight generators to match or even surpass proprietary models on this sophisticated task. Figure 1: Overview of Stride . From K K initial samples, Stride selects a champion and refines it for t t rounds. Each round performs evolutionary refinement and agent state update through dual-route evaluation: the verifier scores candidate images against the rubrics, while the perceptor provides visual grounding of the observed failures. The lead editor then analyzes the agent state and refinement trajectory to route the champion to either the composer for global redraw or the retoucher for local editing. The generated candidates are then re-evaluated, and the champion is updated only when a candidate improves the verifier score. Repeating this process yields the final champion. Agentic Augmentation. Agentic methods ( Wang et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) enhance prompts by retrieving implicit details or reference images to condition generation, but their one-shot rewriting paradigm provides limited constraint enforcement and may overwrite content that is already correct. Methods such as Ag3 ( Hahn et al., 2024 ) and AutoFigure ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) use editable graphs or SVGs to specify image layouts and conduct fixed-round layout-guided refinement. However, their reliance on proprietary models obscures whether gains come from the agentic framework or the base models, which also limits compatibility with most open-weight text-to-image generators. ReflectionFlow ( Zhuo et al., 2025 ) , T2I-Copilot ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and PaperBanana ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) use verifier feedback to assess and refine generated outputs, but the absence of explicit rubric grounding makes failures under-specified, and their reliance on prompt revision or full-image regeneration can disrupt already correct regions and limit reliable improvement. Guided by dual-route evaluated failed rubrics and an evolution strategy, Stride adaptively combines global regeneration with local editing to target specific errors, addressing the above limitations while ensuring stable improvement. 3 Method 3.1 Overview As shown in Figure 1 , Stride is a training-free multi-agent framework designed to iteratively refine images produced by any black-box text-to-image generator G ⁡ ( P , z ) G(P,z) , where P P is a prompt query and z z a noise sample. We observe that generation failures often arise in two opposite regimes: global/compositional errors that local editing cannot repair, and localized residual errors that full re-generation would only perturb. Stride therefore operates over a scale-aware execution space with two complementary sub-agents – a composer that globally resamples the frozen generator and a retoucher that locally edits the current champion. The per-round choice between them is made by a central lead editor , which selects and guides the sub-agent based on the current agent state and the observations from a dual-route evaluation module. The core components of Stride are: (1) Dual-Route Evaluation. Stride uses internal evaluations to drive iterative image refinement. Notably, it decouples evaluation into two complementary MLLM-based modules with distinct roles. The verifier performs closed-form judgment, scoring fine-grained semantic compliance against a rubric set. The perceptor performs open-form grounding, extracting region-level structured descriptions (object locations, rendered text, attribute–region bindings, etc.) that help localize where a failed rubric is violated. Separating judgment from grounding lets each module specialize, and supplies the editor with the spatial evidence a pass/fail score alone cannot provide. (2) Trajectory-Aware Lead Editor . As the central controller, the lead editor maintains a running state of candidate history, prior discriminator observations and failure mode, and the detailed editing history. Rather than simple prompt rewriting, it performs reflective trajectory analysis, makes a decision on which actor (composer or retoucher) to invoke, and then formulates prompt updates for the selected actor that target to address previous failures. (3) Scale-Aware Execution Sub-Agent Space . To prevent generative drift during iterative image generation, Stride operates over a dual-branch action space defined by two sub-agents. The composer explores the global generative manifold by rewriting the prompt and then resampling the image generator G G , while the retoucher identifies localized editing needs and invokes specialized computer-vision tools, guarded by the perceptor’s spatial grounding. The output of each editing action is then admitted or rejected under an evolution strategy. The current champion enters a new round of image refinement, until the iteration budget is exhausted. 3.2 Agent State Stride orchestrates the image refinement process as an iterative loop. At each iteration t t , the system maintains a state tuple S t S_{t} defined as: S t = ( I t , V t , E t , H t ) . S_{t}=\bigl(I_{t},\ V_{t},\ E_{t},\ H_{t}\bigr). Stride separates rubric-based verification from spatial grounding, routes failures to either global composition or local retouching according to their scale, and admits only candidates that improve verifier-scored constraint satisfaction under an evolution strategy. Across BizGenEval, IGenBench and WISE, Stride consistently improves open-weight generators, outperforms prior agentic enhancement methods, and matches or surpasses proprietary systems.
